query: TSMC CoWoS advanced packaging capacity constraints AI accelerators
normalized: accelerators advanced ai capacity constraints cowos packaging tsmc

output.content:
**TSMC’s CoWoS advanced-packaging capacity has been a material near-term constraint on AI-accelerator supply—not merely a supporting production step.** CoWoS is the 2.5D packaging platform that integrates large logic devices/chiplets with high-bandwidth-memory stacks, providing the compute and memory bandwidth required by HPC and AI products. [[1]]

**Why it constrains accelerator shipments:** an AI GPU or ASIC cannot be shipped as a usable high-end accelerator without both leading-edge logic fabrication and sufficient CoWoS/HBM integration capacity; consequently, added wafer-fab capacity does not fully translate into accelerator output if advanced packaging remains unavailable. TSMC’s CEO characterized demand as previously “much, much higher” than it could prepare for, said CoWoS remained fully loaded in April 2025, and said the company still needed substantial new capacity to meet demand. [[2]]

**Demand drivers are structural rather than limited to one chip generation.** TSMC defines its AI-accelerator exposure as data-center AI GPUs, AI ASICs, and HBM controllers, and it said in April 2025 that it expected this revenue category to double in 2025. [[2]] By January 2026, TSMC reported that AI accelerators represented a high-teens percentage of 2025 revenue and raised its expected 2024–2029 AI-accelerator revenue CAGR to the mid-to-high-50% range. [[3]]

**Supply response:** TSMC planned to double CoWoS capacity during 2025, explicitly tying the expansion to customer demand. [[2]] Yet the company’s subsequent comments indicate that expansion was insufficient to eliminate the bottleneck quickly: in October 2025, management said it was still working to narrow the demand/supply gap, would continue increasing capacity in 2026, and that both front-end and back-end capacity related to AI were “very tight.” [[4]] The company allocated 10%–20% of its 2025 capital budget to specialty technologies plus advanced packaging, testing, mask-making and other uses, while total 2025 capex reached $40.9 billion and its 2026 capital budget was set at $52–$56 billion. [[2]] [[3]]

**Technology transition can keep packaging intensity high.** Management described 2025 as predominantly CoWoS-S and indicated a transition toward CoWoS-L in 2026, alongside growing customer uptake of SoIC and more advanced packaging. [[2]] CoWoS-L is designed for larger HPC products and combines chip-on-wafer-on-substrate integration with an RDL interposer and local silicon interconnects, illustrating why each new accelerator generation can demand more complex packaging rather than simply more leading-edge wafers. [[1]]

**Implications for AI-accelerator vendors and investors:** 
- **Revenue timing and unit availability remain packaging-dependent:** vendors with secured CoWoS allocations can convert demand into shipments more reliably, while those without sufficient allocation can face delayed ramps even if chip designs and wafer supply are ready. This follows directly from TSMC’s reported fully loaded CoWoS position and continued demand/supply gap. [[2]] [[4]]
- **The constraint supports TSMC’s strategic value capture:** CoWoS is essential to AI/HPC systems, demand rose markedly after generative AI emerged, and TSMC continues to expand advanced-packaging capacity to support customers. [[1]]
- **Constraint relief is gradual, not instantaneous:** TSMC’s 2025 doubling program and continued 2026 expansion should increase shipment capacity, but management’s October 2025 description of tight front-end and back-end AI capacity suggests allocation and execution—not demand—remain the principal risks to near-term accelerator supply. [[2]] [[4]]

**Bottom line:** CoWoS has evolved into a binding supply-chain gate for cutting-edge AI accelerators because it joins the large leading-edge compute dies and HBM stacks that define modern AI systems. TSMC is investing aggressively and expanding capacity, but its own disclosures show demand remained ahead of available advanced-packaging supply through 2025 and continued to require additional capacity in 2026. [[1]] [[2]] [[4]]
